meta.blurb: After rain, a mushroom pushes up through the leaves, and it is only the fruit of something much larger hidden in the ground. Fungi recycle dead wood, trade with trees, make bread rise, and most kinds have never been named.
meta.bible: Fungi: Spore, Tempeh, Termites, Amphibians, Amphibian. One of the kingdoms of life, along with plants and animals. The singular is Fungus. Key terms: Mushroom, Mycelium, Hyphae, Spores, Enzymes, Lignin, Yeast, Mould, Lichen, Truffle, Puffball, Gills, Mycorrhiza, Mycorrhizal, Fermentation, Carbon, Phosphorus, Nitrogen, Antibiotics, Bacteria, Algae, Alga, Decomposers, Chytrid, Parasitic, Tracer, Mycoremediation, Sawdust, Compost, Foragers, Ciclosporin. Penicillin: found in the mould Penicillium by the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming in 1928 and made into a medicine by other scientists in the 1940s. Ciclosporin: a medicine first found in a soil fungus that helps stop the rejection of transplanted organs. Honey fungus: a huge Armillaria fungus in Oregon, about nine square kilometres, probably thousands of years old; its age is uncertain. Prototaxites: a giant organism about four hundred million years ago, most likely a fungus, though this is debated. Leafcutter ants and some termites farm fungus. A fungus brought by accident to North America killed billions of American chestnut trees in the early 1900s. The Chytrid fungus has harmed amphibians. Never eat a wild mushroom unless an expert has identified it. About 150,000 species of fungi are named, out of an estimated two to three million. The science of mycorrhizal networks between trees is real but debated: scientists disagree about how much it matters in a whole forest. No invented numbers, studies or quotes. Voice: second person, calm, curious, plain and a little amazed; the reader is a walker in a forest after rain.

beats.summary: The body of a fungus is made of hyphae, threads much thinner than a hair.

beats.summary: Hyphae together make a network called a mycelium, which can be enormous in total length.

beats.summary: Fungi digest food outside their bodies with enzymes, then absorb the result.

beats.summary: Decomposing fungi return nutrients to the soil, so new plants can grow.

B1B2: After a night of rain, you walk through the forest and notice a pale mushroom beside the path. It looks small and simple, but it is only a tiny part of something much larger.
Biologists put fungi in a kingdom of their own, beside plants and animals. Mushrooms, yeasts and moulds all belong to it, and so do many living things that nobody ever notices.
It may sound strange, but the family tree of life puts fungi nearer to animals than to plants. Like us, they cannot make their own food from sunlight.
A mushroom is to a fungus what an apple is to an apple tree. It is the part that appears for a short time, while the main body stays hidden in the soil or inside wood.
These threads are called hyphae, and each one is much thinner than a human hair. They grow at the tips, pushing slowly through soil, wood and leaves.
All of these threads together are called a mycelium. In rich soil a single spoonful may hold many metres of them, and scientists think a handful may hold far more.
A fungus does not swallow its food as we do. It releases strong chemicals called enzymes, which break the food down outside the body, and then it absorbs the liquid that results.
A green plant makes its own food from light, air and water, but a fungus has no green leaves and cannot do this. Instead, it must take its food from something else that is alive or dead.
Many fungi are called decomposers, because they live on dead things. They slowly break down fallen leaves, dead wood and the bodies of dead animals into smaller and simpler parts.
Wood is full of a tough substance called lignin, and very few living things can digest it. Wood-rotting fungi are among the best at the job, which is why dead trees do not last forever.
As fungi break down dead material, the minerals and nutrients locked inside are set free. New plants can then use them, so nothing in the forest is truly wasted.
Fungi do not make seeds like plants do, but they make spores. These are single tiny cells, so small that a mushroom can shed millions of them into the air in a short time.
A large puffball is a round white fungus that looks like a football. When it is ripe, a touch makes it puff out a brown cloud that may hold trillions of spores.
If a spore lands somewhere damp and full of food, it sends out a first thread. Often it must meet another thread of the same kind before it can grow into a full fungus.
Fungi grow in many surprising shapes, from umbrellas and shelves to balls and cups. Some look like coral or a honeycomb, and each shape is a different way to spread spores.
These circles are called fairy rings, and old stories said that fairies danced there. In fact, a mycelium grows outward from a centre, and the mushrooms appear at its growing edge.
A mushroom can seem to appear overnight, because the threads below have already built most of it. It swells fast as it takes in water, and a mushroom is mostly water.
Not every fungus makes a mushroom, and yeast is one example. Yeast is a tiny fungus made of just one cell, and when it eats sugar in dough it makes bubbles of gas.
When yeast has no air, it turns sugar into alcohol as well as gas. People discovered this long before they knew yeast existed, and they have made beer and wine for thousands of years.
Some of our foods need other kinds of fungi to be made. Blue cheese gets its veins from a mould, and soy sauce and tempeh are made with moulds that work on beans.
Mould is a kind of fungus too, and its spores are in the air everywhere. They grow fast on damp bread and fruit, so mouldy food is best thrown away.
In 1928, a scientist named Alexander Fleming came back from holiday and found a mould growing on one of his dishes. The germs that had been growing near the mould had all died.
The mould was a type called Penicillium, and its chemical was named penicillin. In the 1940s other scientists learned to make it in large amounts, and it began to save many lives.
Penicillin was not the last medicine from a fungus. A drug called ciclosporin, first found in a fungus in soil, helps stop the body from rejecting a transplanted organ.
Look closely at rocks and tree bark and you may see crusty grey or orange patches. These are lichens, each one a partnership between a fungus and a tiny alga that makes food from sunlight.
Lichens can live where almost nothing else can, on bare rock, in deserts and on cold mountains. Some grow only a tiny amount each year, so a few may be hundreds of years old.
Under the ground, the thin threads of many fungi wrap around plant roots, or even grow inside them. This close partnership is called mycorrhiza, which means fungus-root.
In this deal, the fungus brings the plant water and minerals such as phosphorus. In return, the plant gives the fungus some of the sugar it makes with sunlight.
About nine in ten kinds of land plant have these fungal partners. Tiny fossils suggest that the first plants on land already had them, about four hundred million years ago.
A single fungus can touch the roots of many trees at once. In this way, trees of the same or different kinds may be joined by a hidden underground network.
In some experiments, small amounts of carbon moved from one tree to another through fungi. However, scientists still argue about whether this really helps seedlings or whole forests.
Truffles are fungi that form their fruit underground, usually near tree roots. They have a strong smell, and some kinds are among the most expensive foods in the world.
A buried truffle cannot throw its spores into the wind, so it uses its smell instead. Animals such as squirrels and deer dig it up, eat it and carry the spores away.
In Oregon, a honey fungus spreads through about nine square kilometres of forest. Its age is uncertain, but scientists think it may be thousands of years old.
A few kinds of mushroom give off a faint green light. Scientists think the glow may attract insects, which then help to spread the spores, but they are still testing this idea.
Leafcutter ants cut leaves, but they do not eat them. They carry them to their nest and use them to grow a fungus, which is the food that the ants really eat.
Ants are not the only farmers among the insects. In parts of Africa and Asia, some termites grow fungus inside their nests, and the fungus helps them break down tough plant material.
One fungus infects ants in tropical forests and changes how they behave. The ant climbs a plant and holds on tight, and the fungus then grows out of it to spread its spores.
Fungi can also be a danger to plants and trees. In the early 1900s a fungus arrived in North America by accident and killed billions of American chestnut trees over the next few decades.
A skin fungus called chytrid has spread around the world and harmed frogs, toads and salamanders. It is blamed for the decline of many species, and some may have disappeared completely.
A few fungi can make people ill, and a mild example is athlete's foot, a skin fungus that likes warm and damp places. Most fungi do us no harm, and a doctor can help with any worry.
Some wild mushrooms are deadly poisonous, and some look very much like safe ones. The rule is simple: never eat a wild mushroom unless an expert has identified it for you.
The mushrooms in shops are usually grown on farms. Button mushrooms grow on compost, oyster mushrooms like straw, and shiitake mushrooms grow well on logs or sawdust.
Some kinds of mushroom are easy to grow at home. Oyster mushrooms will grow on used coffee grounds, so a bucket of old coffee can turn into a meal.
About four hundred million years ago, there were giant spires called Prototaxites, taller than a house. Most scientists now think they were fungi, though it is not entirely certain.
The soil holds more carbon than all the air. Scientists think fungi play a large part in keeping some of it safely underground, though they are still learning how much.
Some fungi can break down oil and other pollution, because they use strong enzymes. Researchers are testing them for cleaning up soil, though this work is still at an early stage.
People now grow mycelium in moulds to make useful things. It can form packaging, bricks for building and even material that feels like leather.
Scientists have given names to only about 150,000 kinds of fungi. They think there may be two or three million, so most are still unknown.
You walk back past the pale mushroom, and it no longer looks small. Beneath it lies a living web that feeds, recycles, heals and connects, and most of it is still waiting to be understood.
C1C2: After a night of heavy rain, you walk into the forest and notice a pale mushroom pushing up through the leaves beside the path. It seems small, simple and slightly strange, a thing that appeared overnight without any plan. Yet it is only the visible tip of a living world that mostly stays hidden, and this book will take you underneath it.

Biologists have long recognised fungi as a kingdom in their own right, standing apart from both plants and animals. Mushrooms, yeasts and moulds all belong to it, along with a vast crowd of organisms that most of us never notice. For a long time they were wrongly filed with plants, simply because they grow in the ground and do not move.

It may sound surprising, but studies of DNA place fungi on the same branch of life as animals, much closer to us than to any plant. Like us, they cannot make food out of sunlight, and they have to find it ready-made. The resemblance is old, since the two groups parted ways more than a billion years ago, and it is a reminder that appearances can mislead.

A mushroom is to a fungus what an apple is to an apple tree: a short-lived structure built to spread offspring, not the whole living thing. The main body stays hidden in the soil, in rotting wood or inside a dead leaf, where it may have been growing for years. If you pick a mushroom, you remove the fruit, but the fungus usually carries on below.

The hidden body of a fungus is built from hyphae, microscopic threads that are many times thinner than a human hair. Each thread lengthens only at its tip, so it feels its way forward through the soil, the wood or the leaf litter like a very patient explorer. Along the way it branches again and again, and the single thread becomes a spreading web.

Taken together, the threads form a mycelium, a living network that can stretch through a whole patch of woodland. In rich soil a single spoonful may hold many metres of hyphae, and the total length beneath a forest is almost beyond imagining. Seen under a microscope, it looks less like a plant and more like the plan of a very old, very busy city.

Unlike an animal, a fungus does not take its food inside its body and digest it there. Instead it pours out powerful enzymes that break a leaf or a log down from the outside, and it then absorbs the dissolved nutrients through the walls of its threads. In a sense, the fungus eats by turning the world around it into soup.

A green plant captures sunlight and turns it into sugar, but a fungus contains none of the green pigment needed for that trick. Every fungus is therefore a borrower, depending on dead remains, living hosts or partners to supply the energy it needs. This one fact explains almost everything about how fungi live, from rotting logs to the roots of trees.

Many fungi make their living as decomposers, feeding quietly on fallen leaves, dead branches and the remains of animals. As they feed, they break complicated material into simple substances, and the dead forest floor gradually turns into dark, crumbly soil. It is humble work, and almost no one thanks them for it, yet the whole forest depends on it.

Wood is held together by lignin, a tough and stubborn substance that very few organisms can digest. Certain fungi have the right enzymes to take it apart, and they are among the main reasons that fallen trees slowly crumble instead of lying unchanged for centuries. Wherever you see a soft, crumbling log with brackets growing from its side, you are watching that slow dismantling at work.

When a fungus digests a dead leaf, the nitrogen, phosphorus and other minerals locked inside it are released back into the soil. Young plants can then absorb them through their roots, and the cycle begins again. Without this endless recycling, the world would slowly fill up with dead material, and living things would run out of the building materials they need.

Fungi, unlike the plants they so often grow beside, produce no seeds at all. They spread instead by releasing spores, microscopic cells so light that the slightest breeze can carry them away. A single mushroom can shed millions of them, and if you place a ripe cap on a sheet of paper overnight, you may find a delicate print of its gills in dust.

The giant puffball is a smooth white globe that can grow as big as a football, and when it ripens it fills with brown powder. A single touch, or even a raindrop, makes it puff out a cloud that may hold trillions of spores. Nearly all of them will land in the wrong place, but the sheer quantity gives a few of them a chance.

A spore that happens to fall on a damp, food-rich spot will sprout a first fine thread, and that thread begins to explore. In many species it must meet another compatible thread before the two can fuse and form a full mycelium, which makes the choice of partner a surprisingly careful business. Fungi can have thousands of mating types, far more than the two sexes that animals have.

The fruiting bodies of fungi come in a startling range of shapes, including umbrellas with gills, shelves on tree trunks, balls, tiny cups, branching coral and the pitted honeycomb of a morel. Each design is a different solution to the same problem, which is how to launch spores into moving air. Some are brilliant orange, others are pure white, and a few look like something from a toy shop.

In meadows and lawns, mushrooms sometimes appear in a near-perfect circle, which old folk tales explained as the dancing place of fairies. The truth is quieter and more impressive: a single mycelium has been spreading outward from one point for years, and it fruits where its young edge is most active. Some rings have kept growing for decades, and a few are thought to be much older.

A mushroom can appear overnight, which has encouraged all sorts of old stories about magic. In reality the mycelium has already been preparing a tiny, tightly packed mushroom for days, and when the weather is right the cells swell with water and push it upward. Most of a mushroom is water, so the whole thing can stand up astonishingly fast and then collapse almost as quickly.

Not every fungus builds a mushroom, and yeast is the smallest and most useful example. Each yeast is a single cell, and when it feeds on the sugar in dough it breathes out tiny bubbles of carbon dioxide. Those bubbles are trapped in the stretchy dough, and in the heat of the oven they swell into the soft holes inside a loaf.

When yeast works without much air, it turns sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide, a process we call fermentation. People discovered how to use it long before anyone knew that yeast was a living thing, and brewing and winemaking are among the oldest crafts we know. It is a curious fact that humanity's oldest partnership with a fungus is also one of its most enjoyable.

Many of the world's favourite foods rely on fungi that are carefully chosen and invited in. The blue veins in blue cheese are a mould, soy sauce is made with a mould that works on soybeans and wheat, and tempeh is a firm cake of beans bound together by white threads. In each case the fungus does the cooking slowly, and the flavour comes from what it leaves behind.

Mould is simply a fungus growing in a form that we can see, and its spores drift through every kitchen. On warm, damp food they sprout quickly, spreading threads deep into the bread or fruit well beyond the fuzzy patch on the surface. That is why mouldy food is better thrown away, since some moulds make substances that can make people ill.

In 1928, the Scottish scientist Alexander Fleming returned from a holiday to find that a mould had settled on one of his laboratory dishes. Around it stretched a clear circle where the bacteria he had been growing had died. He had the sense to wonder why, and that moment of curiosity changed the history of medicine.

The mould in Fleming's dish belonged to the group called Penicillium, and the substance it made was named penicillin. It took other researchers more than a decade to purify it and produce it in quantity, but by the 1940s it was being used to treat infections that had once been deadly. Antibiotics still rank among the most important tools of modern medicine, and they began with a fungus.

Penicillin was only the beginning, because fungi are chemists that have been fighting off rivals for hundreds of millions of years. A drug called ciclosporin, first found in a fungus living in the soil, calms the body's defences so that a transplanted organ is not rejected. Many other medicines have come from fungi, and researchers continue to examine them for new ones.

Look closely at old walls, rocks and tree bark and you will often see crusty patches of grey, green or orange. Each is a lichen, a partnership in which a fungus provides the structure and a tiny alga or bacterium living inside it makes food from sunlight. For a long time lichens were thought to be a single organism, and they remain one of the cleverest alliances in nature.

Lichens can survive on bare rock, in deserts and on frozen mountain slopes, places where almost nothing else could gain a foothold. Many grow by only a fraction of a millimetre a year, and the oldest are thought to have lived for hundreds or even thousands of years. By slowly dissolving the rock they cling to, they help to begin the formation of soil.

Below the surface, the threads of many fungi cling to plant roots or grow right inside them, and the partnership has a name, mycorrhiza, which simply means fungus-root. A plant root is thick and clumsy compared with a hypha, but a hypha is slender enough to slip into the tiniest gaps between grains of soil. Together the pair can do what neither could possibly manage alone, and the whole forest benefits from the arrangement.

The arrangement is a trade: the fungus gathers water and minerals such as phosphorus and delivers them to the root, while the plant pays with sugar made in its leaves. Because its threads reach so far, a fungus can find what a root alone could never find. Plants without such partners often grow poorly in poor soils, which shows how much they have come to depend on them.

Roughly nine out of ten kinds of land plant form these partnerships, which makes them one of the most common relationships on Earth. Fossils of some of the first plants to leave the water, about four hundred million years old, already show fungal threads inside their cells. Some scientists argue that plants might never have conquered the land without such helpers.

A single mycelium can attach itself to the roots of many trees at once, and so a whole stand of trees may be wired together by fungal threads. This hidden network has sometimes been called a kind of underground internet, though that phrase is a simple picture and not an exact description. What actually passes along these threads, and how much it matters, is still being worked out.

In certain experiments, carbon marked with a tracer has moved from one tree to another through a fungal link, and some seedlings seem to benefit from the connection. However, other researchers point out that these results come mostly from controlled settings, and that it is not yet clear how much it matters in a real forest. It is a good example of science at work, with a fascinating idea still being tested.

Unlike most mushrooms, truffles keep their fruiting bodies underground, usually among the roots of oak, hazel or other trees. They give off a powerful, earthy smell, and the rarest kinds sell for extraordinary prices, so people train dogs to find them. A truffle is hardly beautiful, being a knobbly lump of earth, but its perfume has made it famous.

A truffle buried in the ground cannot release its spores into the wind, so it must find another courier. Its smell does the work: squirrels, deer and other animals sniff out the ripe fungus, eat it, and later scatter the tough spores in their droppings. It is an elegant bargain, in which the animal gets a meal and the fungus gets a way to travel.

Beneath a forest in the state of Oregon lies a single honey fungus whose threads cover roughly nine square kilometres, an area larger than a thousand football pitches. Estimates of its age vary widely, but many scientists believe it is at least two thousand years old and perhaps considerably older. It is generally regarded as one of the largest living organisms on Earth, and almost all of it is hidden.

A number of mushrooms give off a faint greenish glow, which is easiest to see in a forest on a very dark night. One recent idea is that the light attracts insects that carry away the spores, and experiments with glowing artificial mushrooms support it. The question is not completely settled, but the thought of a living forest quietly shining is hard to forget.

Leafcutter ants march in long columns carrying pieces of leaf, but they do not eat the leaves themselves. The leaf pieces are fed to a fungus that the ants grow in underground gardens, and it is the fungus that feeds the colony. The ants weed their gardens, protect them from other moulds and have farmed this way for millions of years, long before humans invented agriculture.

Ants are not the only farmers, since certain termites in Africa and Asia also tend fungus gardens inside their nests. The fungus breaks down dry plant material that the insects cannot digest alone, and the termites eat both the fungus and the food it has prepared. Both partners have come to need each other so completely that neither can now survive alone.

In tropical forests, a parasitic fungus infects ants and gradually changes their behaviour, driving them to climb a plant stem and clamp their jaws on it. There the fungus grows a stalk from the ant's body and scatters spores onto the ants below. The result sounds like science fiction, but scientists have studied it carefully, and it shows how precisely a fungus can use another living thing.

Fungi are not always helpful, and the story of the American chestnut shows how destructive one can be. A fungus from Asia reached North America by accident in the early twentieth century, and within a few decades it had killed billions of the great trees that once filled the eastern forests. Scientists are still trying, with great patience, to breed chestnuts that can resist it and return to the forests.

A fungus that infects the skin, known as chytrid, has spread across the world and is held responsible for the decline of hundreds of amphibian species. Frogs breathe and drink partly through their skin, so a skin infection is especially dangerous for them. Some species have probably vanished altogether, and scientists are now looking for ways to protect those that remain.

A small number of fungi can infect people, and the mildest and most familiar example is athlete's foot, which thrives in warm, damp places. Most of the millions of fungal species do us no harm at all, though people with weak immune systems need to be more careful. If you have a worry about an infection, you should ask a doctor, since this book is only a general introduction.

Some wild mushrooms are lethally poisonous, and several of the worst look remarkably like harmless ones, which is why even experienced foragers are careful. The death cap, for example, is responsible for most mushroom poisoning deaths, and cooking does not make it safe. The rule is therefore absolute: never eat a wild mushroom unless an expert has identified it in person.

The mushrooms sold in shops are almost always farmed, in cool, dark rooms where the temperature and the damp are carefully controlled. Button mushrooms are grown on compost, oyster mushrooms on straw, and shiitake on logs or blocks of sawdust, with each kind fruiting on the material it would choose in the wild. Mushroom farming is therefore a sensible way of turning farm waste into a nutritious and popular food.

Some mushrooms are surprisingly easy to grow at home, and oyster mushrooms in particular will happily colonise damp, used coffee grounds. A bucket of waste that would have gone into the bin can therefore become a crop of food in a few weeks. It is a small example of how fungi turn what we throw away into something worth having.

About four hundred million years ago, when plants were still small, the land was dotted with huge tower-like organisms called Prototaxites, some of them taller than a house. Their nature puzzled scientists for more than a century, but most now think they were giant fungi, though a few still disagree. If so, the first great landscape of Earth belonged not to trees but to mushrooms.

The world's soils hold more carbon than the whole atmosphere, and the question of how it is stored there has become urgent. Researchers think that fungi, especially mycorrhizal ones, play a large part in locking some of that carbon underground, though the details are far from settled. If so, protecting healthy soil is one of the quiet ways of protecting the climate.

Because fungi dissolve tough natural materials, some of them can also break down pollutants such as oil, and a few have even been seen to attack certain plastics in laboratory studies. The idea of using them to clean contaminated soil, sometimes called mycoremediation, is promising. However, most of this work is still at an early stage, and it is not yet a solution for a polluted world.

Engineers have begun to treat mycelium as a building material, growing it in moulds filled with farm waste until the threads bind everything into a solid block. The resulting material can be used for packaging, insulation, bricks and even a leather-like fabric. It is light and can be composted afterwards, which makes it an attractive alternative to some plastics.

Scientists have so far described only about 150,000 species of fungi, but estimates of the true number run from roughly two to three million. That means the great majority are still unnamed, and a handful of new ones are found every day, often hiding in a single patch of soil. Few corners of nature hold as much undiscovered life as this one, and most of it lies just beneath our feet.

You walk back along the path and pass the pale mushroom again, though it no longer looks small or simple. Beneath your feet lies a living web that recycles the dead, feeds the trees, cures infections and bakes the bread, and much of it is still waiting to be understood. The next time you stand in a forest after rain, you will know that the most active part of it is hidden from view.
